instructional_purpose: Establishes the graphemic inventory of the writing system before any morphology or syntax is attempted: the learner learns to identify every consonant letter in its standalone citation shape, name it, attach an approximate sound value to it, and separate visually identical skeletons by their dot signatures. It is orientation material for a reader with no prior exposure to the script.
concepts_taught: right-to-left writing direction
a fixed inventory of 28 consonantal letters
the standalone shape as the citation shape of a letter
shape families that share one skeleton
dots as the sole discriminator inside a shape family
plain versus emphatic consonant pairing
consonants with no close counterpart in English phonology
letters that will later double as long-vowel carriers (previewed only)
the traditional ordering of the inventory

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The alphabet encodes 28 consonantal letters; vowel quality is carried by separate marks or by carrier letters and not by members of this inventory.
Within a shape family, letter identity is fixed entirely by how many dots there are and whether they sit above, below, or inside the skeleton.
Four plain consonants each pair with a pharyngealized counterpart written with a distinct letter, the pair differing in emphasis rather than in basic place of articulation.
Sound values can be conveyed to an English speaker by approximate English or European analogues.
One emphatic consonant is treated as the identity marker of the language in the traditional epithet for Arabic.
A small subset of letters bears no dots at all and is identified by skeleton alone.

recognition_criteria: locate the shared skeleton first, then count dots and register their placement
read hook-shaped letters by the orientation of the hook plus dot presence
distinguish tall vertical strokes by the presence or absence of a base hook
separate bowl-shaped letters by whether the dot sits above or below the bowl
treat toothed skeletons as one family and use dot count to resolve them
procedures: group the inventory into skeleton families before memorising individual letters
store each letter as a bundle of name, skeleton, dot signature, and approximate sound value
verify dot count and placement before committing to a letter identity
conditions: the dots are legible and the text is not defective, damaged, or in a style that suppresses pointing
exceptions: undotted letters are identified by skeleton alone and have no dot signature to check
three of the letters listed as consonants also serve as long-vowel carriers, a dual role deferred to a later lesson
one letter is described as having several distinct functions rather than a single sound value
contrasts: voiced versus voiceless dental fricatives, written with different dot counts on different skeletons
plain versus emphatic counterparts across four pairs
the light laryngeal h against the pharyngeal one
a deep uvular stop against the ordinary velar stop

common_mistakes.pattern: reading a letter without checking dot count or dot side, so that members of one skeleton family are exchanged for each other
common_mistakes.why_wrong: inside a family the skeleton carries no identity at all; the dots are the whole of the contrast
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat the dot signature as part of the letter, not as an ornament, and read it before naming the letter

common_mistakes.pattern: confusing letters that have similar overall silhouettes but belong to different families, such as two hook-shaped letters that face in different directions or two bowl-shaped letters differing only in dot side
common_mistakes.why_wrong: silhouette similarity across families is accidental and is not resolved by dots alone but by stroke orientation
common_mistakes.correction_principle: anchor identification on orientation and baseline behaviour first, then on dots

common_mistakes.pattern: failing to hold the plain/emphatic pairs together in memory, so the emphatic member is read as its plain partner
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the pairs are phonemically distinct and the emphatic member changes the quality of neighbouring vowels
common_mistakes.correction_principle: learn each emphatic letter explicitly against its plain partner rather than as an isolated item

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the light laryngeal h and the pharyngeal fricative as one letter
common_mistakes.why_wrong: they are separate letters with separate articulations and separate skeletons
common_mistakes.correction_principle: rehearse the two articulations against each other and tie each to its own skeleton

misleading_shortcuts: taking the English sound approximations as exact equivalences rather than as first approximations
assuming a dot difference is decorative
assuming the citation shape is what will be met in running text
assuming that because all 28 letters are called consonants none of them ever represents a vowel
paradigms: family-by-family tables pairing letter, Arabic name, transliteration and approximate value
a complete ordered listing of the inventory in the traditional sequence
exercise_types: multiple choice on dot signature
multiple choice on letter naming and on inventory size
free-response recall of a letter name in transliteration
multiple choice pairing letters by shared property
new_knowledge: the entire grapheme inventory
dot-based discrimination inside skeleton families
the emphatic/plain pairing
writing direction
later_dependencies: positional letter forms
diacritic marks and vocalization
the sun/moon classification of the same inventory
hamza seat letters
root-letter identification in later morphology
sarf_relevance: low - it supplies the grapheme inventory that later root and pattern work presupposes but teaches no morphological content
nahw_relevance: none - there is no syntactic content in the lesson
tutor_drill_relevance: high for absolute-beginner recognition drills: confusable-pair discrimination and letter naming are closed-set and auto-gradable
rich_hover_relevance: low - hover glosses operate over tokens rather than glyphs; at most this supports a script-orientation aside
corpus_pvn_relevance: none directly - letter identity alone yields no particle, verb, or noun entries
required_evidence: only glyph-level identification; nothing here licenses any claim about a token's root, pattern, or grammatical function
uncertainty_flags: the plain/emphatic pairing is a teaching convenience; the historical and articulatory status of the emphatic lateral letter is disputed in the literature
approximate sound values vary across regional pronunciations and reciting traditions, and the lesson gives one neutral value per letter

proposed_new_units.summary: the closed letter inventory together with skeleton families, dot signatures, and the resulting set of confusable letter pairs
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: the catalog begins at root/pattern/affix letter ownership and silently assumes the grapheme layer is already settled; no listed unit represents letter identity, dot signatures, or confusability

new_capability_required: a confusable-grapheme interface (which letters are mutually substitutable under mis-pointing or OCR noise); none of the five consumer families expresses glyph-level confusability

instructional_purpose: Teaches that letters are realized by position-conditioned variants inside a word and that a closed set of letters refuses attachment on its left, so that an orthographic word can break into several connected runs. The learner is trained to identify a letter across its variants and to predict where a word will visually split.
concepts_taught: the four positional variants of a letter
attachment along a baseline, with a right side and a left side
initial, medial, final, and standalone variants defined by which sides attach
the closed set of six letters that never attach leftward
connected runs as the visual segmentation unit inside a word
invariance of dot signature and core skeleton across variants
homography of several medial variants, resolved only by dots

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Most letters have four contextual variants, selected by whether attachment occurs on the right only, the left only, both sides, or neither.
A closed set of six letters never attaches to what follows it, so those letters realize only two of the four variants.
A non-attaching letter forces a break, so one orthographic word may consist of several separately connected runs.
Letter identity is carried by dot signature and core skeleton, both of which persist across all positional variants; only connecting strokes change.
In medial position several distinct letters reduce to the same baseline bump and are separated only by their dots.
The hamza-bearing and the bare forms of the first letter are counted as one member of the non-attaching set.
A non-attaching letter standing at the start of a word can be described indifferently as standalone or initial, since the two shapes coincide for it.

recognition_criteria: read a gap inside a word as the trace of a non-attaching letter rather than as a word boundary
identify a variant by which of its sides bears a connecting stroke
use dot signature to resolve medial bumps that share one skeleton
expect the descending body of certain families to reappear in standalone and final variants and to flatten in initial and medial ones
procedures: mark every member of the non-attaching set in the letter string, then cut the word immediately after each of them to obtain the connected runs
assign each letter its variant by position: nothing before it makes it initial, attachment on both sides makes it medial, nothing after it makes it final, neither makes it standalone
when reading, hold the dot signature constant and let the connecting strokes vary
conditions: the letter is not a member of the non-attaching set
the letter to its right is itself capable of attaching leftward
exceptions: the six non-attaching letters have no initial and no medial variant
a word beginning with a non-attaching letter still opens a run, but with the standalone shape
handwriting may reduce a toothed skeleton to a smooth wave without changing identity
contrasts: a word built only from attaching letters, forming one run, against a word containing non-attaching letters, forming several
the standalone against the final variant of the same letter, which differ only by an incoming stroke
initial against medial variants of the same family

common_mistakes.pattern: attaching a member of the non-attaching set to the letter that follows it
common_mistakes.why_wrong: membership in that set is lexically fixed and blocks leftward attachment regardless of what follows
common_mistakes.correction_principle: memorise the closed set and apply it before deciding any variant

common_mistakes.pattern: reading medial bumps of different letters as the same letter
common_mistakes.why_wrong: in medial position those skeletons are genuinely identical; only the dots carry identity
common_mistakes.correction_principle: in medial position, read the dots first and the skeleton second

common_mistakes.pattern: letting letters drift off the baseline so that attachment level is lost
common_mistakes.why_wrong: attachment is defined relative to a shared baseline; losing it destroys the cue that tells initial from final
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat the baseline as part of the letterform and keep attachment strokes level

common_mistakes.pattern: reading an internal gap as the end of a word
common_mistakes.why_wrong: gaps are produced by non-attaching letters as well as by word boundaries
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check whether the letter before the gap belongs to the non-attaching set before positing a word boundary

misleading_shortcuts: assuming every letter has four visibly distinct shapes
assuming the standalone shape is what appears in running text
assuming a visual gap always separates words
assuming variant choice depends on the letter alone rather than on its neighbours
worked_analysis_stages: a short word is walked letter by letter, each letter labelled with its variant and with whether it attaches forward, to show run formation
paradigms: per-family four-column tables giving standalone, initial, medial, and final variants
a closed enumeration of the non-attaching letters
exercise_types: multiple choice on variant selection
multiple choice on membership in the non-attaching set
free-response counting of connected runs in a word
fill-in-the-blank on the term for positional shape
error-diagnosis multiple choice on an illegal attachment
prerequisite_knowledge: the grapheme inventory and dot signatures from the preceding lesson
reuses_from_earlier: L1.M1.01 letter inventory
L1.M1.01 shape families and dot discrimination
new_knowledge: positional allography
the attachment class of a letter
segmentation of a word into connected runs
later_dependencies: reading fully vocalized text
the dotless yaa seat used for hamza
the word-final-only distribution of the tied taa
any orthographic normalization or tokenization over surface forms
sarf_relevance: low - positional shape is orthographic rather than morphological, though run boundaries affect how a reader picks root letters off a surface form
tutor_drill_relevance: high - variant identification and run counting are mechanical, closed-set, and auto-gradable
rich_hover_relevance: low to medium - relevant to rendering and to aligning a hover span with a token, not to gloss content
corpus_pvn_relevance: none directly - this affects surface-form storage and normalization rather than which entry kind a token belongs to
required_evidence: an attachment-class table plus the letter sequence; no morphological or syntactic evidence is needed and none is licensed
uncertainty_flags: ligature behaviour, notably the obligatory laam-alif ligature, is neither covered nor derivable from the rules as stated
font and handwriting styles differ in how strongly variants are differentiated, so visual criteria are approximate

proposed_new_units.summary: a closed two-way classification of letters by whether they attach leftward, plus the derived segmentation of a word into connected runs
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: every catalog unit operates above the grapheme layer; none encodes attachment behaviour, positional variants, or run segmentation, yet these determine what a surface form looks like

instructional_purpose: Introduces the three short-vowel diacritics as marks attached to consonants rather than as letters, fixes their shapes and above/below placement, and explains that ordinary written Arabic omits them so that readers must recover vowels from context, from word patterns, and from grammatical endings.
concepts_taught: harakaat as diacritics rather than letters
the a-mark, the u-mark and the i-mark with their names and placements
consonant plus mark read as one CV unit
the genres in which full vocalization is normative
the vocalized versus unvocalized state of a text
preview of the vowellessness mark

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Each short vowel is written as a mark bound to a consonant and is pronounced after that consonant.
Two of the three marks sit above the consonant and one below; two of them share essentially the same stroke shape, so placement is their only visual discriminator.
Ordinary prose omits these marks, and competent readers restore them from context, from knowledge of word patterns, and from grammatical endings.
Full vocalization is normative for scripture, for beginners' material, for poetry, for teaching material, and wherever a form would otherwise be ambiguous.
The Arabic name of each mark is motivated by the articulatory gesture that produces the vowel.
An unmarked consonant is not automatically vowelless, since a separate mark exists for vowellessness and since a following carrier letter may be involved.

recognition_criteria: a short oblique stroke above a consonant versus the same stroke below it
a small hook resembling a miniature wow-letter above the consonant
absence of any mark, which signals either vowellessness, an unvocalized text, or a carrier configuration rather than a default vowel
procedures: work through the word from right to left, reading each consonant together with the mark written on it
when transliterating, emit the consonant then the vowel of its mark
when a consonant carries no mark, do not supply a vowel by guesswork
conditions: the text is vocalized
the consonant actually bears a mark
exceptions: a consonant may legitimately bear no vowel at all, marked separately
a short-vowel mark followed by its matching carrier letter yields a long vowel rather than a short one, which is deferred to the next lesson
contrasts: the above-placed against the below-placed oblique stroke
short vowel against its lengthened counterpart
vocalized against unvocalized text conventions

common_mistakes.pattern: exchanging the a-mark and the i-mark
common_mistakes.why_wrong: they are near-identical strokes and are distinguished only by whether they stand above or below the letter
common_mistakes.correction_principle: read placement before shape whenever an oblique stroke appears

common_mistakes.pattern: pronouncing the u-mark as a long back vowel
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the mark encodes a short vowel; the long counterpart requires an additional carrier letter
common_mistakes.correction_principle: keep short vowels short and reserve length for marked carrier configurations

common_mistakes.pattern: inserting a vowel after a consonant that bears no vowel mark
common_mistakes.why_wrong: vowellessness is a real, separately marked state, and inserting a vowel changes the syllable structure and can change the word
common_mistakes.correction_principle: only pronounce a vowel where a vowel mark licenses one

common_mistakes.pattern: expecting every Arabic text to carry vowel marks and stalling when it does not
common_mistakes.why_wrong: unmarked text is the normal case, and the marks are supplied by the reader from pattern and syntax knowledge
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat vocalization as recoverable information rather than as a property of the page

misleading_shortcuts: equating the short u-vowel with a long English back vowel
assuming any unmarked letter is vowelless
assuming that mark-free text is defective or informal
treating the etymological name-glosses as phonetic descriptions
worked_analysis_stages: several fully vocalized words are split into syllables and read mark by mark to model the consonant-plus-mark reading routine
paradigms: a grid crossing a set of common consonants with all three marks to give every CV combination
exercise_types: multiple choice on identifying a mark and its placement
free-response transliteration of a single CV syllable
applied reading of short fully vocalized words
free-response identification of the vowel repeated across a word

L1.M1.02 letter shapes in context

sarf_relevance: medium - templates in later morphology are stated in terms of exactly these vowels, and the routine absence of the marks in real text is the structural reason morphological analysis is needed at all
nahw_relevance: low - the marks that will later realize case and mood are introduced here, but no syntactic function is attached to them yet
tutor_drill_relevance: high - mark identification, placement, and CV transliteration are mechanical and closed-set
rich_hover_relevance: medium - a hover gloss normally needs a vocalized citation form that the running text does not itself supply, which is precisely the gap this lesson names
corpus_pvn_relevance: cross-cutting over p, v and n: every entry kind needs both a vocalized citation form and an unvocalized surface key, since real text supplies only the latter
required_evidence: assigning a vowel to an unmarked consonant in running text requires template or syntactic evidence; orthography alone gives none
uncertainty_flags: the phonetic value of each vowel shifts next to emphatic consonants and across reciting traditions, while the lesson gives one neutral value
partially vocalized text, which is common in practice, is not addressed

proposed_new_units.summary: the three short-vowel marks with their placement rules, plus the fully/partially/un-vocalized state of a token and what each state licenses
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: no catalog unit represents the diacritic layer or the vocalization state of a surface form, although every sarf and nahw unit implicitly assumes vowels are known

new_capability_required: a vocalization-state interface (is this token fully vocalized, partially vocalized, or bare, and which marks are actually attested) - none of the five consumer families expresses it

instructional_purpose: Introduces the two marks that are not vowels: the mark of vowellessness, which closes a syllable, and the gemination mark, which doubles a consonant. The learner is taught to keep the two apart visually and to understand gemination as two consonant slots rather than one heavier letter.
concepts_taught: the vowellessness mark and the vowelless letter
the voweled versus vowelless status of a consonant
open and closed syllable types
the gemination mark and the process it names
the terms for a geminated letter
gemination combined with a following short vowel
gemination produced by assimilation of the definite article (previewed)
meaning contrasts created purely by gemination

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A small circle above a consonant marks that no vowel follows it, so that consonant closes its syllable.
The gemination mark means the consonant is realized twice: a vowelless first instance closing one syllable and a voweled second instance opening the next.
A gemination mark normally co-occurs with a short-vowel mark, and that vowel is read after the doubled consonant, not between its halves.
Gemination is contrastive: doubling the middle consonant of a verb yields a different derived form with a different meaning.
When the definite article precedes one class of letters, the article's laam assimilates and the result surfaces as a gemination mark on the following consonant.
The vowellessness mark tends to fall on the final consonant of short function words and on syllable-closing consonants inside stems.
Failure to realize gemination produces a different existing word rather than a mispronunciation of the intended one.

recognition_criteria: a hollow circle above a consonant, versus a small w-shaped mark
a short-vowel mark stacked above or below the gemination mark
a gemination mark on the first consonant of a noun standing immediately after the definite article, which signals assimilation rather than lexical doubling
a consonant with no mark at all in a vocalized text, which is not the same as one bearing the circle
procedures: on meeting the circle, pronounce the consonant and move straight to the next sound without inserting any vowel
on meeting the gemination mark, expand it into two consonant slots and attach the accompanying vowel to the second slot
before treating gemination as part of the stem, check whether it stands right after the definite article and is therefore assimilatory
when transliterating, write the geminated consonant twice
conditions: the text is vocalized, since both marks are routinely omitted in ordinary prose
the geminated consonant is not word-initial, so that its first half has a syllable to close
exceptions: gemination introduced by the definite article belongs to the clitic boundary, not to the noun's stem
a geminate that carries no following vowel mark, as at the end of some short words, cannot be split across two syllables in the same way
contrasts: the hollow circle against the w-shaped mark
single against doubled consonant in otherwise identical words
a vowelless consonant against the first half of a geminate, which are phonetically alike but orthographically distinct
a verb without gemination against the same root with a geminated middle consonant

common_mistakes.pattern: mistaking one mark for the other because both are small superscript signs
common_mistakes.why_wrong: they encode opposite things: one says no vowel follows a single consonant, the other says the consonant is doubled and a vowel follows
common_mistakes.correction_principle: read the shape deliberately - a closed circle versus an open w-shape - before assigning a value

common_mistakes.pattern: pronouncing a geminated consonant once
common_mistakes.why_wrong: gemination is contrastive, so collapsing it substitutes a different word with a different derived form
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat the gemination mark as licensing two consonant slots and hold the consonant accordingly

common_mistakes.pattern: inserting a vowel after a consonant that bears the vowellessness mark
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the mark exists precisely to forbid that vowel, and inserting one alters the syllable count
common_mistakes.correction_principle: the circle is a prohibition, not a neutral placeholder

common_mistakes.pattern: realizing the gemination but ignoring the vowel written with it
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the accompanying vowel determines the syllable that follows the doubled consonant and therefore the word's ending
common_mistakes.correction_principle: always read the gemination mark together with any vowel mark stacked on it

misleading_shortcuts: treating the gemination mark as expressive emphasis rather than as a segmental instruction
assuming every geminate belongs to the lexical stem
assuming a consonant with no mark must be vowelless
assuming a vowelless consonant and a geminate half are the same object
worked_analysis_stages: a geminated verb is decomposed into syllables to show that the doubled consonant is shared between two syllables
paradigms: a two-row comparison of the two marks by shape, name and effect
a list of high-frequency function words that carry the vowellessness mark
a list of high-frequency stems that carry gemination
exercise_types: multiple choice on identifying a mark and its effect
free-response recall of the Arabic term for a geminated letter
fill-in-the-blank transliteration of a series of words containing each mark

reuses_from_earlier: L1.M1.03 short vowels and the notion of a voweled consonant
L1.M1.01 consonant inventory
new_knowledge: the vowelless state as a marked category
syllable typology, open versus closed

sarf_relevance: high - the geminate/vowelless distinction is the notational basis for handling doubled roots and for telling a Form I verb from a Form II verb
nahw_relevance: low - several emphatic and negating particles that appear in the word lists are syntactically loaded, but no syntax is taught here
tutor_drill_relevance: high - mark identification, gemination expansion, and transliteration are all mechanical and auto-gradable
rich_hover_relevance: high - a gloss that drops or misplaces gemination will name the wrong derived form and often the wrong lexeme
corpus_pvn_relevance: all three kinds: vowelless-final function words as p entries, Form II verbs whose identity rests on the geminated middle radical as v entries, and doubled-root nouns as n entries
required_evidence: projecting a derived-form claim from a gemination mark requires that the mark be actually present and lexical rather than assimilatory; bare text supplies no gemination evidence at all
uncertainty_flags: both marks are omitted in ordinary prose, so their absence on the page is not evidence of their absence in the spoken form

instructional_purpose: Teaches that each short vowel has a long counterpart formed by a matching carrier letter, that length is contrastive, and that two of the three carriers are graphemically identical with consonants, so the learner must be able to tell a carrier from a consonantal radical. It also introduces the word-final variant spelling of long a.
concepts_taught: lengthening as the relation between a short vowel and its long counterpart
the three carrier letters and their pairing with the three short vowels
the carrier as an unmarked letter with no segmental value of its own
phonemic vowel length
the carrier versus consonant reading of two of the carriers
the word-final variant spelling of long a
duration as roughly double that of the short vowel

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A long vowel is a short vowel followed by its matching carrier letter; the carrier contributes duration, not an additional segment.
Each of the three short vowels selects exactly one carrier letter, and the pairing is fixed.
Vowel length is phonemic: shortening or lengthening a vowel yields a different word.

Two of the carriers are the same graphemes as two consonants, and the discriminator offered is whether the letter bears a vowel mark of its own: unmarked after the matching short vowel means carrier, marked means consonant.
A word-final undotted yaa-shaped grapheme is to be read as long a rather than as long i.
Which of the two spellings of final long a a word takes is conditioned by the historical identity of its final radical.
In classical copies the carrier yaa may appear undotted while modern printing keeps its dots, so dotting is a convention rather than a reliable cue.

recognition_criteria: an unmarked alif immediately after a consonant carrying the a-mark
an unmarked wow-letter immediately after a consonant carrying the u-mark
an unmarked yaa immediately after a consonant carrying the i-mark
a word-final dotless yaa-shaped grapheme
a wow-letter or yaa bearing its own vowel mark, which blocks the carrier reading
procedures: on meeting one of the three carrier graphemes, look one letter to its right: if that consonant carries the matching short vowel and the carrier itself carries no mark, read a long vowel
if the candidate carrier carries its own vowel mark, read it as a consonant instead
hold a long vowel roughly twice the duration of its short counterpart
for a word-final a-sound, choose the variant spelling on the basis of the word's underlying final radical rather than by ear
conditions: the preceding consonant carries the matching short vowel
the carrier itself carries no mark
the text is vocalized, since the whole test is stated over marks
exceptions: the variant final spelling of long a occurs only in word-final position
in unvocalized text the carrier-versus-consonant test cannot be applied at all, because it is stated entirely over marks that are absent
contrasts: short against long vowel in otherwise identical consonant frames
a carrier wow-letter or yaa against a consonantal one
the two spellings of word-final long a
a verb form against a participle differing only in vowel length

common_mistakes.pattern: reading every wow-letter or yaa as a vowel, or conversely as a consonant, without checking marks
common_mistakes.why_wrong: both letters are genuinely ambiguous between the two roles, and the role determines both pronunciation and, later, whether the letter is a radical
common_mistakes.correction_principle: decide the role from the mark configuration - own vowel mark means consonant, unmarked after the matching vowel means carrier

common_mistakes.pattern: pronouncing the word-final variant spelling of long a as long i because it looks like a yaa
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the grapheme is a positional variant of the a-spelling, not a yaa, despite the shared skeleton
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat a word-final dotless yaa-shaped grapheme as the a-spelling unless there is evidence to the contrary

common_mistakes.pattern: shortening long vowels in speech
common_mistakes.why_wrong: length is contrastive, so shortening substitutes a different lexeme
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat duration as part of the phoneme and rehearse minimal pairs deliberately

misleading_shortcuts: reading any occurrence of the two ambiguous letters as a vowel by default
treating vowel length as a matter of style or emphasis
assuming the mark-based carrier test is usable on ordinary unvocalized text
assuming dotting reliably separates the final a-spelling from a final yaa

paradigms: a three-row correspondence table mapping short vowel to carrier to long value
minimal-pair sets contrasting short and long vowels
a structured table-completion item over the same three-way correspondence
exercise_types: multiple choice on which vowel and carrier combine
multiple choice on which letter carries a given long vowel
free-response recall of the Arabic term for lengthening
fill-in-the-blank pattern completion
a paradigm-table completion item
prerequisite_knowledge: the three short-vowel marks and their placement
the consonant inventory and positional forms
reuses_from_earlier: L1.M1.03 short vowels
L1.M1.04 vowellessness as the state of an unmarked-but-marked letter
L1.M1.01 the dual-role letters previewed in the inventory
new_knowledge: the carrier relation and the three long vowels
the carrier-versus-consonant discriminator
phonemic length

nahw_relevance: low - two very common prepositions are cited as examples of the final a-spelling, but no syntax is taught

instructional_purpose: Introduces nunation: the three doubled-vowel endings that add a nasal to a noun, the writing rule that the a-form normally needs a silent supporting alif, the three graphemic environments that exempt it, and the claim that nunation marks a noun as indefinite and cannot co-occur with the definite article.
concepts_taught: nunation as a written doubled vowel mark pronounced as vowel plus n
the three nunation forms

nunation as distinct from gemination

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Nunation is written as a doubled short-vowel mark and pronounced as that vowel followed by a nasal.
There are exactly three nunation marks, one built on each short vowel.
The a-form of nunation normally requires a supporting alif which is written but never pronounced.
The supporting alif is omitted when the word already ends in the tied taa, in a hamza already seated on alif, or in the variant final a-spelling.
Nunation marks a noun as indefinite and is therefore incompatible with the definite article.
The supporting alif is a preserved orthographic residue of the historical accusative ending.
Nunation is a different phenomenon from gemination even though both are informally described as doubling.

recognition_criteria: a doubled vowel mark on the final letter of a nominal
a final alif carrying a doubled a-mark, where the alif is not pronounced
a doubled mark placed directly on the tied taa with no added alif

procedures: identify the doubled mark, read its base vowel, then append the nasal

apply all three forms to one noun to drill the ending contrast while the stem stays constant

instructional_purpose: Develops the definite article as an invariantly written but variably pronounced clitic: fourteen letters trigger assimilation of its laam, realized as gemination of the following consonant, and fourteen do not. The learner is trained to classify any letter into the two groups and to pronounce accordingly.
concepts_taught: the definite article as a written prefix marking definiteness
invariance of the written article against variability of its pronunciation

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The definite article is written identically in every case but has two pronunciations conditioned by the first consonant of the following word.
Fourteen letters cause the article's laam to assimilate, so the laam is written but not pronounced and the following consonant is geminated.
The other fourteen letters leave the laam audible and take no gemination mark.
The triggering set is phonetically coherent, consisting of tongue-tip articulations, while the non-triggering set gathers the remaining places.
The two class names are mnemonic, taken from the canonical noun of each class rather than from any property of the letters.
The split is exactly half and half across the inventory.
Adding the article removes nunation, since the two markers cannot co-occur.

recognition_criteria: a gemination mark on the consonant immediately following the article
a vowelless laam followed by an unmarked consonant, which signals the non-assimilating class
classification decided by the first consonant of the following word and by nothing else
procedures: look up the following word's first letter in the two-way classification, then pronounce the article accordingly
when vocalizing, give the laam the vowellessness mark before a non-triggering letter and instead place the gemination mark on a triggering letter
when speaking, double the triggering consonant rather than merely dropping the laam
conditions: the definite article is actually present as a prefix
the classification is applied to the first consonant of the following word
contrasts: an article-prefixed word with a triggering initial against one with a non-triggering initial
the written form of the article, which never varies, against its spoken form, which does

common_mistakes.pattern: pronouncing the laam before a triggering letter
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the laam is orthographic only in that environment; pronouncing it produces a form no speaker uses
common_mistakes.correction_principle: let the class of the following letter, not the spelling, decide what is pronounced

common_mistakes.pattern: adding gemination to a non-triggering letter by analogy
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the non-triggering class takes no gemination and keeps an audible laam
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply the classification in both directions rather than generalizing the assimilation case

common_mistakes.pattern: dropping the laam but failing to double the triggering consonant
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the assimilated laam is not deleted but merged into the following consonant, which is why that consonant lengthens
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat assimilation as merger, so the material is preserved as gemination

common_mistakes.pattern: mixing up which letters belong to which class
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two classes are closed sets that must be known exactly, since nothing in the spelling reveals membership
common_mistakes.correction_principle: anchor membership on the articulatory generalization and rehearse the closed lists

assuming the written article always corresponds to an audible laam
assuming the articulatory generalization partitions the inventory exactly
assuming assimilation is optional or stylistic

instructional_purpose: Separates the two word-final spellings of the same consonant: the tied grapheme, restricted to word-final position and normally marking feminine gender, and the open grapheme, used where the consonant is a root letter, a subject suffix, or part of a plural pattern. It also teaches the context-dependent realization of the tied grapheme and both classes of exception to the gender inference.
concepts_taught: two graphemes for one consonant

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Two distinct graphemes render the same consonant; one of them occurs only word-finally.
The tied grapheme is the productive feminine marker: suffixing it derives the feminine of many adjectives and of agent-type nouns.
The tied grapheme is realized as t when a case ending is pronounced or when the word is the first member of an annexation, and as h or as nothing in pausal position.
The open grapheme is used where the consonant belongs to the root, is a verbal subject suffix, or is part of a plural pattern, and it is always realized as t.

A set of nouns denoting titles or professions carries the tied grapheme while being grammatically masculine, the grapheme there being traditionally analysed as an intensifier rather than a gender marker.
In two very common feminine nouns ending in the open grapheme, that consonant is presented as belonging to the root itself.

Projecting the lesson's root assignment for those two nouns into a root field would place a feminine-marking consonant among the radicals, against the standard triliteral analysis in which the final radical is a weak letter that has dropped.
The tied grapheme never occurs word-internally, so a medial occurrence of the consonant is always the open grapheme.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the spelling of the glottal stop: that it is a consonant which usually rides on a seat letter, and that the seat is selected by the hamza's position in the word together with a ranking of the surrounding vowels. It gives separate rules for word-initial, medial and final position and notes several special configurations.
concepts_taught: the glottal stop as a consonant distinct from the vowel-carrying alif
the seat as the letter that carries the hamza
the four seat options including the seatless one
a strength ranking over the three vowels and vowellessness

the combined alif-plus-hamza grapheme
the connecting word-initial alif that carries no hamza

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The glottal stop is a consonant whose written realization requires a seat letter chosen by position and by surrounding vowels.
Word-initially the seat is always alif, and only the placement of the hamza above or below it varies with the vowel.
Word-medially the seat is determined by the stronger of the vowel on the hamza and the vowel on the preceding letter, on the ranking i over u over a over vowellessness.
Word-finally only the vowel on the preceding letter matters, and after vowellessness or after a long vowel the hamza takes no seat.
A hamza cannot be seated on a letter that is itself functioning as a long vowel, which is why the seatless form appears there.
A word-initial hamza with the a-vowel following an alif merges with it into a single combined grapheme.
A class of words begins with a connecting alif that bears no hamza mark, is pronounced with a glottal stop only utterance-initially, and elides after a preceding word.
In certain medial environments after a long vowel the hamza is written on the line, and the alternative seated spellings are treated as incorrect.
The yaa-shaped seat is written without dots and has its own name.

recognition_criteria: a hamza mark above or below an alif at the start of a word
a hamza riding on a wow-letter or on a dotless yaa-shaped seat

procedures: classify the hamza's position as initial, medial or final
for initial position, write alif as the seat and place the hamza below it only for the i-vowel, above it otherwise
for medial position, read the vowel on the hamza and the vowel on the preceding letter, rank them, and take the seat associated with the stronger
for final position, read only the preceding vowel and take its seat, or write the hamza seatless if that vowel is long or absent
when in doubt, enumerate the surrounding vowels explicitly before choosing
conditions: the surrounding vowels are known, which in practice means the environment is vocalized
the hamza is of the cutting type rather than the connecting word-initial alif
exceptions: after a long vowel the hamza is seatless even where the strength ranking would otherwise predict a seat
hamza with the a-vowel after an alif merges into the combined grapheme instead of taking a seat
words with a connecting initial alif carry no written hamza at all
contrasts: seated against seatless hamza
hamza-bearing alif against plain carrier alif
the dotless hamza seat against an ordinary yaa
cutting against connecting word-initial alif
hamza placement above against below the initial alif

common_mistakes.why_wrong: the seat is fully determined by position plus the vowel ranking, so guessing discards available information
common_mistakes.correction_principle: always enumerate the two relevant vowels and apply the ranking before writing

common_mistakes.pattern: placing the hamza below the initial alif with a vowel other than the i-vowel

common_mistakes.pattern: giving the hamza a seat when it follows a long vowel

common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat a preceding long vowel as an absolute trigger for the seatless form

instructional_purpose: A capstone that applies every orthographic device of the module jointly to whole words and short sentences. It supplies a letter-by-letter analysis routine for reading fully vocalized text and an ordered production routine for writing it, and it labels the nunation endings with case names for the first time.
concepts_taught: joint resolution of all diacritic devices within one word
a tabulated letter-by-letter analysis routine

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The devices of the module co-occur in ordinary words and must be resolved jointly rather than one at a time.
The three nunation endings correspond to the three grammatical cases, here named for the first time in the module.
A vocalized word can be produced in a fixed order: consonant skeleton, connections, short vowels, vowellessness, gemination, then any ending.
The tied grapheme is realized without the t in pause and with it in connected speech.
Gemination changes the count of consonant segments in a word, so a geminated form has one more consonant slot than its ungeminated counterpart.
Whether the definite article's laam is audible is read off the class of the following letter, which can be checked directly on a vocalized form by looking for a gemination mark.
Fully vocalized text is sufficient for accurate reading, so mastery of these marks completes the reading toolkit.

recognition_criteria: a gemination mark on the letter after the article, indicating assimilation rather than lexical doubling
a doubled vowel mark at the word edge, indicating an indefinite ending rather than a plain vowel
a long vowel identified as a short-vowel mark plus an unmarked matching carrier
a word-final tied grapheme carrying a case vowel or a nunation mark
a seatless hamza following a long vowel
procedures: tabulate the word letter by letter, recording each letter with the mark it carries
assign a value or a function to every mark before pronouncing anything
decide the article's behaviour from the class of the following letter
syllabify the analysed word, then produce a transliteration
when writing, follow the fixed order: skeleton, connections, short vowels, vowellessness, gemination, ending
conditions: the input is fully vocalized, since every step of the routine reads a mark
the token has been segmented from any attached clitic before analysis
exceptions: the a-form of nunation is written without its support after the tied grapheme
hamza following a long vowel takes no seat regardless of the ranking
the tied grapheme is realized differently in pause and in connection, so a single transliteration is context-bound
contrasts: short against long vowels in near-identical consonant frames
assimilating against non-assimilating article environments in worked examples
the three nunation endings against one another under case labels
a geminated against an ungeminated form of the same stem

common_mistakes.pattern: reading past the gemination mark and pronouncing a single consonant
common_mistakes.why_wrong: gemination adds a consonant slot, so ignoring it changes both the segment count and often the derived form
common_mistakes.correction_principle: count the doubled consonant twice when segmenting or transliterating

common_mistakes.pattern: reading a nunation ending as a plain short vowel
common_mistakes.why_wrong: nunation contributes a nasal in addition to the vowel, and its absence changes the ending's grammatical value
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check whether the final mark is single or doubled before pronouncing the ending

common_mistakes.pattern: pronouncing the article's laam before an assimilating letter
common_mistakes.why_wrong: in that environment the laam merges into the following consonant, which is why that consonant is geminated
common_mistakes.correction_principle: read the gemination mark on the following letter as the signal that the laam is not pronounced

common_mistakes.pattern: realizing the tied grapheme with a t when the word stands in pause
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the t realization is conditioned by a following ending or an annexed word, neither of which is present in pause
common_mistakes.correction_principle: let the following context, not the grapheme, decide the realization

common_mistakes.pattern: guessing a hamza seat instead of deriving it
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the seat is determined by position plus the ranked surrounding vowels, all of which are visible in vocalized text
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply the ranking explicitly rather than relying on visual familiarity

common_mistakes.pattern: inserting a vowel after a consonant carrying the vowellessness mark
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the mark forbids a following vowel and defines a closed syllable
common_mistakes.correction_principle: treat the mark as a prohibition and keep the syllable closed

misleading_shortcuts: assuming that because the input is vocalized no analysis is needed
treating the pausal transliteration of a word as its only form
assuming the writing order is merely a study habit rather than a way of avoiding omitted marks
assuming that mastering the marks is sufficient for reading the unvocalized text learners will actually meet

sarf_relevance: low - no new morphology is introduced; the lesson drills accurate reading of forms whose morphology is treated elsewhere
nahw_relevance: low - case labels appear on the nunation paradigm for the first time but are given no syntactic account, and the sentence exercises ask for orthographic features rather than for parsing
tutor_drill_relevance: high - the analysis routine and the writing order convert directly into staged, auto-gradable drill templates with per-stage checkpoints
rich_hover_relevance: medium - the letter-by-letter tabulation is a plausible model for an expandable hover detail view, though its content is orthographic rather than semantic
corpus_pvn_relevance: mainly n, since the worked examples are nunated and article-prefixed nouns; v and p appear only incidentally in the sentence exercises
required_evidence: the whole routine presupposes fully vocalized input; on bare text every stage would require external morphological or syntactic evidence that this lesson does not provide
uncertainty_flags: the pausal versus connected realization rule for the tied grapheme is stated without the case-ending condition that actually governs it
case names are introduced as labels on endings with no assignment rules, which invites treating case as a property of the ending rather than of the syntactic position
the closing claim that these devices suffice for reading any text holds only for vocalized text

proposed_new_units.summary: an ordered analysis routine for reading a fully vocalized word and an ordered production routine for writing one, with per-stage checkpoints
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: the catalog models tables and classifications, not ordered procedures; this lesson's yield is a staged method that no listed unit and no consumer family currently represents
